what_its_for: Abrocitinib is used to treat moderate-to-severe eczema (also called atopic dermatitis) in adults and teenagers 12 years and older whose eczema is not well controlled with other treatments. It works by blocking certain proteins in your body (called JAK1) that cause inflammation and itching.
how_to_take: Take abrocitinib by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, split, or chew it. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. If you take antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox or Mylanta), take abrocitinib at least 2 hours before taking the antacid.
dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is 100 mg once daily. Your doctor may increase your dose to 200 mg once daily if your eczema is not well controlled. For teenagers (12 to 17 years old), the dose is based on weight and your doctor will decide the right amount. Always take the exact dose your doctor prescribed — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and just take your regular dose that day. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store abrocitinib tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from moisture, heat, and light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who have active infections, such as chickenpox, shingles, or the flu, since abrocitinib can weaken your immune system. Avoid getting live vaccines (such as the live shingles vaccine Zostavax or nasal flu spray vaccine) while taking this medicine — talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine may slightly increase your risk of certain skin cancers. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine, as it may harm an unborn baby — use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after stopping.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to an emergency room if you have: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, sweating, muscle aches, cough, shortness of breath, or painful urination; signs of a blood clot such as sudden leg pain or swelling, chest pain, or difficulty breathing; unusual tiredness, pale skin, or dizziness (may be signs of low blood counts); stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting that does not go away; any new or unusual skin changes or lumps; symptoms of shingles such as a painful skin rash or blisters. Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
when_it_works: Some people notice their itching improves within the first 2 weeks of treatment. Skin clearing may take longer — usually 4 to 12 weeks of regular use. Do not stop taking this medicine on your own even if you do not see immediate results. Talk to your doctor if your symptoms do not improve after several weeks.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): Use with caution, as older adults may have a higher risk of serious infections and certain side effects. Kidney problems: Your doctor may lower your dose or may not recommend this medicine if you have moderate-to-severe kidney disease. Liver problems: This medicine is not recommended if you have severe liver disease. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use abrocitinib if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it may harm your baby. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Teenagers (12 to 17 years): Can be used in teenagers weighing at least 25 kg (about 55 lbs), but the dose will be determined by your doctor. Children under 12 years: Safety and effectiveness have not been established in younger children.
